title: 纠偏旧账：MobyGames 允许开发者认领未被署名的作品
content:
Righting old wrongs: MobyGames on letting developers claim games they weren't credited for | GamesIndustry.biz

In March 2022, Atari acquired the video game database MobyGames.
It was a surprise move for this latest iteration of the long-lived publisher, which has in the past few years
put its focus on retro
. At the time,
CEO Wade Rosen highlighted MobyGames' role in the "documentation, celebration, and preservation of video games"
, and later said there were
plans for the database
.
Now, we have some idea of what those plans are. In June, MobyGames
announced a new paid tier
to its offering, geared towards industry professionals. MobyGames Professional is currently available in beta – with a 1.0 version set to launch in autumn – and it allows users to, among other things, claim video game credits, customise their personal portfolio, and track in-demand skills and salaries in their discipline.
Reece Denzel  |
Image credit:
MobyGames
In an interview at Gamescom, product manager Reece Denzel tells
GamesIndustry.biz
that signups to the platform have been "great", adding that "thousands of developers" have claimed their pages on the service.
"Developers, or anybody who is working in the industry who has game credits, have had those public-facing profile pages for a very long time," Denzel says. "There's now a claim page button, which allows for the association of that user's account to the actual public-facing page. It's very important for us to note that that does not give them the ability to edit any of the structural information about things like their credits. What it does give them the opportunity to do is to go in and edit some details about themselves that are then listed as coming from the verified source of that developer."
Cases of people being left off game credits are
well documented
, and the new function potentially allows users to claim titles for which they are otherwise uncredited. However, it could also potentially open up MobyGames to bad actors, who claim credit for games they never worked on. To stop that, the firm has rolled out a verification process.
"There's two parts to that," says Denzel. "One is making sure that people are who they say they are, and that's a human-driven verification process that we run in the background. When it comes to making sure that credit history is reflected appropriately, the actual way that we do credits and credit verifications has not changed: It's not changed since Atari has been involved, it's not changed in a long time, and we have no plans to change that process.
"There are some times where we need to go back and make corrections, and it's usually around cases where people might have names that are misspelled, or they go by a different name at some point. And those are things that we have processes to correct. But ultimately our guiding goal is that information that is on the site is as accurate as humanly possible, which is not necessarily always 100%, but it's about as close to 100% as it can be."
Community work
Much of the work on maintaining MobyGames' database of games and developers is done by volunteers, or as Denzel puts it, "a very active contributor and approver community".
"The credits often come from things like screenshots from the credit roll after the game," he explains. "Sometimes we'll have companies send us spreadsheets from a more official source, but a lot of it is community-sourced and community-verified." He calls it a symbiotic relationship: a system maintained by the community, for the community.
MobyRank shows which games and genres are most popular according to page views  |
Image credit:
MobyGames
There's also MobyRank, which allows users to see how popular certain genres or kinds of games are based on page views. But perhaps the most interesting new feature of MobyGames Professional is the ability for developers to create a portfolio page, where they can post about their own work.
"If they're a designer, they want to post either demo reels or screenshots of their work and associate that with the games credits that they have," Denzel says. "They can also write much more lengthy and detailed descriptions of their work, posting links to coverage of their own work or to the writeups, things like their personal site or anywhere that they want to direct users. Our goal there is to connect the verified credit history through MobyGames with the ability for those individuals to promote their work."
He gives the example of an employer discovering that a certain person was a lead designer on a specific game, and then being able to easily see other examples of their output via the designer's portfolio and the MobyGames database.
Job listings
Alongside the games and people database, MobyGames also keeps a database of jobs in the industry pulled from "a variety of locations", says Denzel.
"What that allows us to do is to associate those jobs with the studios in our database, and we can pull elements from those job postings or the ongoing projects from those studios," he explains.
"We can match different elements of those to people who have MobyGames Professional accounts, because we know what the work history is, the genres, the platforms, the number of titles that they've worked on, everything in their credit details and their credit titles. We can serve them up a more personalised look at all the opportunities."
Users can now add a game to their portfolio page, giving details such as exactly what contributions they made  |
Image credit:
MobyGames
The system can also highlight other people who have worked at the same studios as you in the past, or who have provided support for those studios, which could be useful for finding a point of contact or finding someone who can vouch for your skills.
